■ Training objective — maximize the likelihood of the training corpus.

 $$ arg\max_{\theta}\prod_{x\in D_{train}}P_{\theta}(x) $$

## Cross-Entropy Loss

■ Negative log-likelihood over next-token predictions

 $$ arg\max_{\theta}\prod_{x\in D_{train}}P_{\theta}(x)=arg\min_{\theta}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{x\in D_{train}}\sum_{i=1}^{t}-\log p_{\theta}(x_{i}|x_{<i}) $$ 

■ Cross-Entropy Loss: lower is better

 $$ L_{C E}(\theta)=-\log p_{\theta}(x_{i}|x_{<i}) $$ 

The capital of France

 $$ \begin{array}{r} is:0.9\\ are:0.1 \end{array} $$ 

The capital of France

 $$ \begin{array}{r} is:0.4\\ \times 10.6 \quad are:0.6 \end{array} $$ 

 $$ \begin{array}{l}L_{C E}(\theta_{1})=-l o g(0.9)\approx0.1\quad\textcircled{8}\bullet\end{array} $$ 

 $$ L_{C E}(\theta_{2})~=~-l o g(0.4)~\approx~0.9 $$

<!-- page: 8 -->

## Empirical Risk

How much loss should we expect when predicting the next token in new text?

## Population risk R( $ \theta $)

Expected loss per token on new text drawn from the target distribution.

Empirical risk

Estimate that loss using the text in the training corpus.



 $$ -\log p_{1}(capital) $$ 

 $$ -log p_{2}(of) $$ 

 $$ -\log\mathsf{p}_{3}(\mathsf{F r a n c e}) $$ 

 $$ -log\,p_{4}(is) $$ 

 $$ -\mathrm{l o g}\;p_{5}(\mathsf{P a r i s}) $$ 

 $$ \hat{R}(\theta)\;=\;\frac{1}{N}\;\sum_{i=1}^{N}\;\ell_{i}(\theta) $$ 

N counts the target tokens in the training corpus.

## Gradient Descent

- Calculate the gradient of the loss function with respect to the parameter

 $$ \frac{\partial L(\theta)}{\partial\theta} $$ 

■ Update  $ \theta $ by taking a small step along the negative gradient to decrease the loss

 $$ \theta^{new}\leftarrow\theta^{old}-\eta\frac{\partial L(\theta)}{\partial\theta} $$ 

■  $ \eta $ is the learning rate

<!-- page: 11 -->

Projection of Error Surface on 2-dimensional plane

## Why Does Gradient Descent Work?

## Intuition

■ The gradient gives the local slope of a smooth loss surface.

■ At a point with nonzero gradient, a sufficiently small step along the negative gradient lowers the loss.

■ Near a stationary point, the gradient becomes small.

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_1405_516_2622_1151.jpg" alt="Image" width="45%" /></div>

<!-- page: 12 -->

## Learning Rate

The learning rate sets the size of each update.

A small learning rate can require many updates to reduce the loss.

A large step can overshoot the low point and increase the loss.

## SGD + Momentum

Momentum adds part of the previous step to the current SGD step.

A sequence of updates

SGD

SGD + Momentum

 $$ \theta_{t}\;=\;\theta_{t-1}\;-\;\eta g_{t} $$ 

 $ g_{t} $ is the mini-batch gradient,  $ \eta $ is the learning rate, and  $ \rho $ is the fraction of the last step retained.

<!-- page: 15 -->

## Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam)

Each weight has a mini-batch gradient, $g_{t}$

First moment

 $$ m_{t}=\beta_{1}m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_{1})g_{t} $$ 

The signed average sets the direction.

 $$ \widehat{m}_{t}\:=\:m_{t}\left/\left(1-\beta_{1}^{t}\right)\right. $$ 

Second moment

 $$ v_{t}=\beta_{2}v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_{2})g_{t}^{2} $$ 

The mean square sets the scale of the step.

 $$ \hat{v}_{t}=v_{t}/(1-\beta_{2}^{t}) $$ 

Update each weight

 $$ \theta_{t}\;=\;\theta_{t-1}\;-\;\eta\;\frac{\widehat{m}_{t}}{\sqrt{\widehat{v}_{t}}\;+\;\varepsilon} $$ 

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_2033_1021_2387_1335.jpg" alt="Image" width="13%" /></div>


Hats correct for the bias from starting both averages at zero. A small  $ \varepsilon $ keeps the denominator positive.

<!-- page: 16 -->

## How Do We Compute the Gradient?

Let's recall some basic calculus.

The derivative measures how sensitive the output is to a small change in the input.

 $$ f^{\prime}(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} $$ 

Power rule

 $$ f(x)~=~x^r\quad\Rightarrow\quad f^{\prime}(x)~=~rx^{r-1} $$ 

Exponential

 $$ \frac{d}{dx}e^{x}\;=\;e^{x} $$ 

Sum rule

 $$ (\alpha f+\beta g)^{\prime}\;=\;\alpha f^{\prime}+\beta g^{\prime} $$ 

 $ \alpha $ and  $ \beta $ are real constants.

Product rule

 $$ (fg)^{\prime}\;=\;f^{\prime}g+fg^{\prime} $$ 

Chain rule

 $$ f(x)~=~h(g(x))~~\Rightarrow~\quad f^{\prime}(x)~=~h^{\prime}(g(x))~\cdot~g^{\prime}(x) $$

<!-- page: 17 -->

## How Do We Compute the Gradient?

## Gradient of multivariate scalar-valued functions

For a differentiable function with one output, the gradient collects one partial derivative per input.

 $$ \begin{array}{c}f\colon\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R},\qquad f(\boldsymbol{x})\;=\;f(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})\\\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x})\;=\;\begin{bmatrix}\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_{1}}(\boldsymbol{x})\\ \vdots\\ \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_{n}}(\boldsymbol{x})\end{bmatrix}\end{array} $$ 

## Gradient of multivariate vector-valued functions

For m outputs and n inputs,

the Jacobian has m rows and n columns.

 $$ \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})=\left[f_{1}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}),\ldots,f_{m}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})\right] $$ 

 $$ \frac{\partial\boldsymbol{f}}{\partial\boldsymbol{x}}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial f_{1}}{\partial x_{1}}&\cdots&\frac{\partial f_{1}}{\partial x_{n}}\\ \vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ \frac{\partial f_{m}}{\partial x_{1}}&\cdots&\frac{\partial f_{m}}{\partial x_{n}}\end{bmatrix} $$ 

 $$ \left(\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{f}}{\partial\boldsymbol{x}}\right)_{ij}=\frac{\partial f_{i}}{\partial x_{j}} $$ 

Local Jacobians

 $$ \frac{\partial}{\partial\boldsymbol{x}}(\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{b})=\boldsymbol{W}\quad\frac{\partial}{\partial\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{b})=\boldsymbol{I}\text{(identity matrix)} $$ 

 $$ \frac{\partial}{\partial\boldsymbol{u}}\Big(\boldsymbol{u}^{\mathrm{T}}\boldsymbol{h}\Big)\;=\;\boldsymbol{h}^{\mathrm{T}} $$

<!-- page: 18 -->

## Calculate gradients of composite functions: chain rule

Neural networks are compositions of functions.

■ For composition of one-variable functions: multiply derivatives

Each derivative measures how one step responds to its input.

 $$ \begin{aligned}z&=3y\\y&=x^{2}\end{aligned} $$ 

 $$ \frac{dz}{dx}=\frac{dz}{dy}\frac{dy}{dx}=(3)(2x)=6x $$ 

■ For multiple variables at once: multiply Jacobians

The outer function's Jacobian is the left factor in the product.

 $$ \begin{aligned}\boldsymbol{h}&=f(\boldsymbol{z})\\\boldsymbol{z}&=\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{b}\end{aligned} $$ 

 $$ \frac{\partial\boldsymbol{h}}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{h}}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=\cdots $$

<!-- page: 19 -->

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_954_418_2345_769.jpg" alt="Image" width="52%" /></div>


 $$ \begin{aligned}\boldsymbol{s}&=\boldsymbol{u}^{\mathrm{T}}\boldsymbol{h}\\\boldsymbol{h}&=f(\boldsymbol{z})\\\boldsymbol{z}&=\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{b}\\\boldsymbol{x}&\quad(input)\end{aligned} $$ 

 $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\partial s}{\partial x}&=\frac{\partial s}{\partial h}\frac{\partial h}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\\&=u^{T}diag\big(f^{\prime}(z)\big)W\end{aligned} $$ 

(Element wise activation)

<!-- page: 20 -->

## Backpropagation on a Computational Graph

Apply the chain rule in reverse order.

 $$ \begin{aligned}\boldsymbol{s}&=\boldsymbol{u}^{\mathrm{T}}\boldsymbol{h}\\\boldsymbol{h}&=f(\boldsymbol{z})\\\boldsymbol{z}&=\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{b}\\\boldsymbol{x}&(\text{input)}\end{aligned} $$ 

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_1040_693_2384_1198.jpg" alt="Image" width="50%" /></div>


 $$ \begin{array}{ccc}x\longrightarrow&\underset{W}{\bullet}\quad\underset{W x}{\longrightarrow}&+\\&\underset{b}{\longrightarrow}\quad&\frac{\partial s}{\partial\overline{z}}\\W&&\underset{\overline{\partial}\overline{b}}{\longrightarrow}\end{array}\overset{z}{\longrightarrow}\overset{f}{\underset{\overline{\partial}\overline{h}}{\longrightarrow}}\overset{h}{\longrightarrow}\overset{S}{\underset{u}{\longrightarrow}} $$ 

The blue terms show the gradient flow through the graph.

<!-- page: 21 -->

Backpropagation Through an Activation Function

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_329_306_2321_1347.jpg" alt="Image" width="74%" /></div>


Chain rule: downstream gradient = upstream gradient  $ \times $ local gradient.

<!-- page: 22 -->

## Linear Layer: Weight and Input Gradients

For a mini-batch, the linear layer computes $Y = XW$.

The optimizer uses the weight gradient. The input gradient flows to the preceding layer.

Single input

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_160_685_1207_1434.jpg" alt="Image" width="39%" /></div>


## Mini-batch

Weight gradient $(H_{1}\times H_{2})$

 $$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial W}=X^{T}\frac{\partial L}{\partial Y} $$ 

Input gradient  $ (\mathrm{B} \times \mathrm{H}_{1}) $

 $$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial X}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial Y}\;W^{T} $$

## Automatic Differentiation in PyTorch

## Automatic differentiation records the computation graph during the forward pass

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_207_562_1150_769.jpg" alt="Image" width="35%" /></div>


Modules as Building Blocks

class Net2(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(
            self.layer0 = MyLinear(4, 3)
            self.layer1 = MyLinear(3, 1)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.layer0(x)
        x = F.relu(x)
        x = self.layer1(x)
        return x

net2 = Net2()
sample_input = torch.randn(4)
print(net2(sample_input))

## Training Loop in PyTorch

One training step PyTorch
Forward pass  $ \rightarrow $ Batch loss
Backward pass  $ \rightarrow $ Weight gradients
Optimizer step  $ \rightarrow $ Updated weights loss.backward()
inputs, targets = ids[:, :-1], ids[:, 1:]
logits = model(inputs)
loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.transpose(1, 2), targets,
ignore_index=pad_id)
optimizer.step()
optimizer.zero_grad()

## Data Parallelism

Each replica trains on a different part of the same mini-batch.

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_179_541_2395_1240.jpg" alt="Image" width="83%" /></div>


Each GPU needs to store a copy of the entire model.

<!-- page: 31 -->

$$ \begin{array}{ccc}rank0&rank1&rank2\\ \text{in}0&\text{in}1&\text{in}2\\ &\text{in}2&\text{in}3\\ \end{array}\xrightarrow{\quad}&\begin{array}{ccc}rank0&\text{rank1}&rank2\\ \text{out}&\text{out}&\text{out}\\ \text{out}[i]&=\displaystyle\sum in_{r}[i]\\ \end{array}\begin{array}{ccc}rank3&rank4&rank5\\ out&out&out\\ \end{array} $$ 

## Computation and Communication in Data Parallelism

## Sum AllReduce

Global batch

C FLOPs, split evenly

Model replicas

≈ C/K FLOPs per GPU

Local gradients

N elements per GPU

## AllReduce

Equal-token mean

Global Mean Gradient

 $$ \overline{{g}}_{t}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i_{1}=1}^{B_{1}}\nabla f(w_{t};\xi_{i_{1}})+\cdots+\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i_{K}=1}^{B_{K}}\nabla f(w_{t};\xi_{i_{K}}) $$ 

B_{k} is the valid-token count on GPU k. B is the total.

## Estimating KV Cache Memory

Model configuration

 $$ L=80, $$ 

 $$ H_{\mathrm{k v}}=8, $$ 

 $$ d_{\mathrm{h}}\;=\;128, $$ 

 $$ b=2\ \mathrm{bytes}/\mathrm{element} $$ 

KV cache per token

 $$ 2LH_{KV}d_{h}b~=~2\times80\times8\times128\times2\mathrm{B}~=~327,680\mathrm{B}~=~320\mathrm{KiB} $$ 

KV cache at 8,192 tokens per request

One request

 $$ 8,192\times320Ki B=2.5Gi B $$ 

32 concurrent requests

 $$ 32\times2.5G i B=80G i B $$ 

Model weights and temporary buffers need additional memory.
